title: Place Splitter
context: Grade 4, and the first place in the chapter where a division is read rather than worked. An adult sees digits being cut off the end of a number. What is actually being taught is why the cut falls where it does: ten goes exactly into every ten, so only the ones can be left over, and a hundred goes into every hundred, so only the last two digits can be. A child who has learnt the cut as a trick puts it in the wrong place the first time the divisor changes, and copies a remainder with a zero in front of it, which the chapter's own table does once.

writeup.why: Watch a division pattern grow a zero at a time, then cut a number into a quotient and a remainder by where its digits fall.
writeup.look: A number in digit cards under place headings, a splitter bar above it, two trays below it, and a pattern ladder at the left.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Place Splitter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the cuts made against the cuts this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each pair of trays fills or each rung is written, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The pattern ladder stands at the left of the working area, 250 by 480 at 64,214, four rungs one above the other, each holding a dividend in deep blue, the divisor in amber and a quotient slot, the bottom rung filled from the start with a fact that leaves nothing over. Adding a zero to the dividend writes the next rung up. A zero added to the divisor as well is allowed, and that rung writes the same quotient as the rung below it with nothing marked. The digit cards stand across the rest of the top, five columns 130 wide at 350,240, each card under its own place heading from ten thousands to ones. The splitter bar hangs on a rail above them, 650 by 14 at 350,222, and its three setting keys reading ten, a hundred and a thousand are stacked at the right, each 130 by 50 from 1010,240; a setting drops the bar that many cards in from the right hand end, one for each zero in the divisor, and the count of zeros is written on the key as it is pressed. Under the cards the quotient tray, 380 by 96 at 350,384, takes the digits left of the bar in green, and the remainder tray, 250 by 96 at 750,384, takes the digits right of it in vermilion; the digits slide straight down in the columns they came from, and each tray writes what it holds under itself as one number. The front zero lift sits on the remainder tray's left edge and carries a zero standing in front of the remainder's other digits out to a saucer, 130 by 96 at 1010,384, at full size, and a zero with a digit to its left stays in the tray. The bundle view runs under the trays, 650 by 190 at 350,496, drawing the same number as bundles of a thousand, a hundred and ten and loose sticks; the whole bundles of the divisor light with the quotient tray and the loose ones with the remainder tray. The one control, 130 by 50 at 1010,560, runs the same number divided by one, and every finished cut is kept as a small card in a row across the foot, 650 by 36 at 350,694, so the four answers of one number can be read side by side. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a quotient or a remainder is asked for. Its zero key writes a zero in its own place and never slides the other digits along. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A cut never changes the number. The digits drop into their trays in the columns they came from, so no digit is ever seen to change its place on the way, and the trays stay under the cards until the next number is loaded.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last number the child cut, the bar where it fell, both trays filled, and the pattern ladder standing beside it.

phases.win: each rung fills with a quotient one zero longer than the rung below it
phases.does: adds a zero to the dividend, keeps the divisor, and writes the new quotient on each rung
phases.goal: ten times the dividend gives ten times the quotient when the divisor stays the same and nothing is left over
phases.says: Put a zero on the dividend. Keep the divisor. What happens to the answer?
phases.check: Fifty-six divided by eight is seven. What is five thousand six hundred divided by eight, and what stayed the same?
phases.feels: the divisor stayed still, and every zero the dividend gained turned up on the answer
phases.hands: Write forty-eight divided by six is eight on the board. Under it write four hundred and eighty divided by six, and ask for the answer before anyone works it out. Then write four hundred and eighty divided by sixty and ask again. Let the class find that the second answer is eight, and ask what changed between the two.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which number gained a zero? Second rung, the phase's: did the divisor change? Third rung: the ladder is cut to two rungs, twenty divided by five and two hundred divided by five, and the child fills the upper one. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a zero was added to one number, and adding it to both looks like keeping the pattern tidy.
wrong.move: adds a zero to the divisor as well as the dividend and expects the quotient to grow.
wrong.screen: the rung is written as the child set it, with a zero on both numbers, and its quotient comes out equal to the rung below it, twelve beside twelve. The rung above is then written with the divisor left alone, its quotient one zero longer, and both rungs stand together with nothing marked.

wrong.why: the first step up the ladder was one zero on and one zero on, and the second step is heard as the same single move made once more.
wrong.move: adds one zero to the quotient when the dividend has gained two, writing a hundred and twenty for eight thousand four hundred divided by seven.
wrong.screen: the rungs are walked from the bottom one at a time, each adding one zero to the dividend and one to the quotient, with the count of zeros written beside each number. The child's answer stays on its rung beside the one the ladder builds, and seven times it is written under it, eight hundred and forty, beside the eight thousand four hundred it should have made.

phases.screen: the pattern ladder with one division fact on its bottom rung and the rungs above it empty
phases.soWhat: Ten times the dividend gives ten times the quotient when the divisor stays the same and nothing is left over.
phases.concept: A zero on the dividend, a zero on the quotient

phases.win: the loose sticks and the ones digit light together in the remainder tray
phases.does: drops the bar, then matches the two trays to the bundles of ten and the loose sticks
phases.goal: divided by ten, the ones digit is the remainder and the digits in front are the quotient
phases.says: Ten goes into every ten. What is left that cannot make another ten?
phases.check: Away from the screen: bundle sixty-four sticks in tens. Say the quotient and remainder of sixty-four divided by ten first.
phases.feels: the loose sticks are the ones digit, and every bundle of ten is already in the digits in front of it
phases.hands: Give a group seven bundles of ten sticks and eight loose ones. Ask how many whole tens they have and how many sticks cannot make another ten. Write seventy-eight and ask where the answer was hiding in it. Then add a bundle of a hundred and ask again.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many zeros does ten have? Second rung, the phase's: which sticks cannot make another ten? Third rung: the number is cut to two digits, and the bundles are laid out under it before the bar drops. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: numbers are read from the left, and the first thing split off looks as if it ought to be the first digit.
wrong.move: takes the first digit as the remainder because it is the one read first.
wrong.screen: the bar drops at the ten setting, one card in from the right, and the bundle view lights the whole bundles of ten with the quotient tray and the loose sticks with the remainder tray. The bundles the child's digit stands for, seven bundles of a hundred, are lit beside the eight loose sticks, and the child's digit stays in the slot with nothing marked.

wrong.why: the remainder came out as one digit, so the quotient is expected to be one digit too.
wrong.move: writes the quotient as the single digit next to the bar, three, instead of the whole number in front of it.
wrong.screen: the quotient tray writes its digits under itself as one number, seventy-three, and the bundle view counts the tens out: seven hundreds are seventy tens, and three more tens make seventy-three. The child's three stays beside the tray, and ten threes add eight is written under it, thirty-eight, beside the seven hundred and thirty-eight it should have rebuilt.

phases.screen: a three-digit number in cards with the splitter set to ten and the bundle view open
phases.soWhat: Divided by ten, the ones digit is the remainder and the digits in front are the quotient.
phases.concept: Ten splits off the ones digit

phases.win: both cuts stand one above the other, the bar one place further left for the thousand
phases.does: cuts at a hundred, then moves the bar one place left for a thousand and cuts again
phases.goal: divided by a hundred the last two digits are the remainder, and by a thousand the last three
phases.says: How many zeros does the divisor have? Cut off that many digits.
phases.check: Divide four thousand nine hundred and thirty-two by a hundred, then by a thousand. Say where the bar falls each time.
phases.feels: one more zero in the divisor, one more digit that cannot make a whole one of it
phases.hands: Write a four-digit number large on a strip of paper. Ask how many zeros a hundred has, and fold the strip back that many digits from the right. Read the two parts aloud. Then unfold it and fold again for a thousand, and ask why the fold moved one place to the left.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many zeros does this divisor have? Second rung, the phase's: how many digits does that cut off from the right? Third rung: the bar is set to ten first and then moved to a hundred, one card at a time, with the bundles counted at each stop. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the first cut learnt was one digit for ten, and one digit sounds like the rule rather than the first case of it.
wrong.move: cuts off one digit whatever the divisor, instead of one digit for each zero in it.
wrong.screen: the bar drops where the child placed it, one card in, and the trays read eight hundred and twenty-five and four. The check under the trays multiplies a hundred by eight hundred and twenty-five, adds four, and stands the eighty-two thousand five hundred and four it builds beside the eight thousand two hundred and fifty-four. Both stay drawn, and the zeros on the setting key are then counted one at a time.

wrong.why: the digits cut off are the ones the bar was dropped to find, so they feel like the answer being asked for.
wrong.move: writes the two trays the wrong way round, giving the last two digits as the quotient.
wrong.screen: the trays are read back with their names lit, and the check multiplies a hundred by the child's quotient, fifty-four, and adds eighty-two: five thousand four hundred and eighty-two stands beside the eight thousand two hundred and fifty-four, plainly different. The bundle view then fills the trays in its own order, whole hundreds first and loose sticks last, with the child's answer still written.

phases.screen: a four-digit number with the splitter at a hundred and its thousand setting waiting
phases.soWhat: Divided by a hundred the last two digits are the remainder, and by a thousand the last three.
phases.concept: A hundred takes two digits, a thousand takes three

phases.win: the front zero is set aside and the remainder settles, written the way any number is
phases.does: reads the remainder tray, lifts the front zero off, and writes the remainder as a number
phases.goal: a zero in front of a remainder's other digits changes nothing and is not written
phases.says: Read what is in the tray as a number. Does the front zero change it?
phases.check: Divide twenty-three thousand and forty-five by a thousand. Write the remainder the way any number is written.
phases.feels: the zeros in front were holding no place at all, and the number reads the same without them
phases.hands: Write forty-one thousand and seven on the board and cover all but its last three digits. Ask the class to read what is showing the way they would read a price. Then write the remainder of the division by a thousand the way any number is written, and ask what the two zeros were doing.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the remainder tray read as a number? Second rung, the phase's: which zero is standing in front of the other digits? Third rung: the tray is cut to two digits, a zero and a seven, and the child reads it as a price before writing it. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the rule says the last three digits are the remainder, and a table in this chapter prints one remainder that way, as zero one six, when it is the number sixteen.
wrong.move: writes the remainder with its zeros in front, copying the three digits the bar cut off.
wrong.screen: the front zeros lift off one at a time into the saucer at full size, and the number written under the tray does not change as each one goes. The child's remainder stays written beside it exactly as it was entered, and the tray's reading is then written into the answer slot under it, seven, the way any number is written.

wrong.why: zeros have just been lifted off and shown to change nothing, so every zero in the tray looks as if it can go.
wrong.move: lifts every zero out of the remainder, the one in the middle as well, and writes fifty-six for five hundred and six.
wrong.screen: the lift takes only a zero standing in front of the other digits, and the zero with a five on its left stays in the tray, lit and at full size. The bundle view counts what the remainder holds, five bundles of a hundred and six loose sticks, and the child's fifty-six is laid out beside it as five tens and six, plainly fewer. Both stay drawn.

phases.screen: a five-digit number cut by a thousand, with a zero standing first in the remainder tray
phases.soWhat: A zero in front of a remainder's other digits changes nothing and is not written.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the front zero is lifted. The zero rises off the remainder tray and walks to the saucer at full size, the digits left behind do not move a hair, and the number written under the tray does not change by so much as a letter. Put the zero back and it changes nothing again. Lift a zero that has a digit on its left and the lift will not take it; that zero stays lit in the tray, and the bundle view under it shows the hundred it is holding open. The lifting can be done as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the pattern ladder stands at the left with one division fact on its bottom rung and the three rungs above it empty, the divisor already written on each. On the second a three-digit number stands in its cards with the bar set to ten and hanging over the right hand end, and the bundle view under the cards shows the bundles of ten and the loose sticks not yet sorted. On the third a four-digit number stands with the bar on its hundred setting, not yet dropped, and the thousand key waiting beside it. On the fourth a five-digit number is already cut by a thousand, with three digits in the remainder tray and a zero standing first among them. The running count at the top left holds the cuts made against the cuts this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the lowest empty rung, or the bar, or the thousand key, or the front zero, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many zeros the divisor has. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number up to five digits, all three splitter settings and the one control, with the bundle view and the pattern ladder open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on continuing a pattern, dividing by ten, a hundred and a thousand, and writing a remainder the way a number is written.

observations.why: Ten times as much shared among the same number of parts puts ten times as much in each part.
observations.soWhat: A zero on the dividend puts a zero on the quotient only while the divisor stays the same and nothing is left over.
observations.observe: Each rung of the ladder held a quotient one zero longer than the rung below, while the divisor stayed put.

observations.why: Ten goes exactly into every ten in the number, so only the ones cannot make another ten.
observations.soWhat: Divided by ten, the ones digit is the remainder, and that is a fact about bundles rather than a trick with the end of a number.
observations.observe: The loose sticks and the ones digit lit together in the remainder tray.

observations.why: A hundred goes exactly into every hundred and a thousand into every thousand, so one more place is left over each time.
observations.soWhat: Cut off one digit for every zero in the divisor.
observations.observe: The bar moved one card further left each time the divisor gained a zero.

observations.why: A zero standing in front of a number's other digits is holding no place that anything needs.
observations.soWhat: A remainder is a number, so sixteen is written as sixteen and never with zeros in front of it.
observations.observe: The zero lifted off the front of the remainder, and the tray wrote the same number without it.

serves.exercise: completing the second and third division patterns

source_tool.description: A number stands across the stage as a row of digit cards, each under its own place heading. A splitter bar hangs above it with three settings, ten, a hundred and a thousand, and each setting drops the bar that many digits in from the right hand end: one digit for ten, two for a hundred, three for a thousand, one for every zero in the divisor. The digits left of the bar slide down into a quotient tray and the digits right of it into a remainder tray. The remainder tray reads what it holds as a number, so a zero standing in front of the other digits is lifted off, set aside and shown to change nothing, and the remainder is written as any number is. A bundle view under the cards shows the same number as bundles of a thousand, a hundred and ten and loose sticks, so the cut can be seen as the bundles that make whole groups and the sticks that cannot. A pattern ladder at the left starts from one division fact that leaves nothing over and adds a zero to the dividend a rung at a time, keeping the divisor fixed, and the quotient gains a zero on every rung. A one control runs the same number divided by one, so the four answers of one number can be laid side by side.
source_tool.art_direction: Digit cards under a hanging splitter bar / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a tray of counters and a row of plates, digit cards under place headings, sticks tied in bundles, a long division frame with its bracket, a ladder of multiples, a strip of cells, a story card, and two rails tied at every stop.

Equal shares are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a plate or a part is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are on it, and anything counted one at a time is drawn in rows of ten so that no more than twenty loose things ever have to be counted singly.

What is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the shares, in a dish or a slot of its own, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never tucked under a share and never left to be guessed from a gap.
A division is always written with every place headed. The number being divided at a step is shown with its place name, so fifteen tens is never drawn as a bare fifteen.

Every zero in a quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as the other digits and is never dimmed, shrunk or dropped. A zero is written only where the number being divided is smaller than the divisor, and a leading zero may stand or be left off, but a zero after the first digit always stands.
What is left at every step is drawn in its own slot before the next digit comes down, and it slides down to join that digit so the next number can be seen being made.
A remainder is written as a number. A zero standing in front of its other digits is lifted off and set aside, never written into the answer.
No stage ever shows a number for a division by zero. Where one is asked, the stage says it is not possible and draws nothing to share into.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a counter, a digit or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; and what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion. Those four hold from the plates to the frame to the story card in every tool of this chapter. A multiple of the divisor, whether it is being tried on the ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose, so the chunks can be added up without being mistaken for the share. A zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey, and grey never means faint: it is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, because it is holding a place. All of that holds in greyscale, because what is left over is told apart by the dish or the left slot it sits in, and a quotient digit by the row it sits in, before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: A zero on the dividend, a zero on the quotient
Ten splits off the ones digit
A hundred takes two digits, a thousand takes three

placement.where: After a number has been laid out in bundles of ten and a hundred by hand and the whole bundles counted. The tool is what keeps the bundles and the written digits on the stage together while the cut is made, so the cut is seen to be the bundles and not a trick with the end of a number.

answer_key.rule: When the divisor stays the same and the division leaves nothing over, ten times the dividend gives ten times the quotient, so each zero added to the dividend adds a zero to the quotient. Divided by ten, the ones digit is the remainder and the number formed by the digits in front of it is the quotient. Divided by a hundred, the last two digits form the remainder and the rest form the quotient. Divided by a thousand, the last three digits form the remainder. One digit is cut off for every zero in the divisor. A remainder is a number, so any zero standing in front of its other digits is not written: the last three digits zero, zero and seven make the remainder seven. Divided by one, a number is its own quotient with nothing left over.
answer_key.wrong: The bundles are laid out again under the digits, the whole bundles of the divisor are counted into the quotient tray and the loose ones into the remainder tray, and the bar is dropped once more. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 840 is ten times 84, and the divisor has not changed.
84 divided by 7 leaves nothing over, so ten times the dividend gives ten times the quotient, and 12 becomes 120.
One more zero on the dividend puts one more zero on the quotient, so 8400 divided by 7 is 1200.
items.answer: 840 divided by 7 is 120, and 8400 divided by 7 is 1200
items.question: 84 divided by 7 is 12. Use the pattern to find 840 divided by 7 and 8400 divided by 7.
items.checkpoint: Each zero added to the dividend adds a zero to the quotient, while the divisor stays the same and nothing is left over.
items.misconception: Adding a zero to the divisor as well, which leaves the quotient at 12.

steps: Ten goes exactly into every ten in the number, so only the ones can be left over.
The ones digit, 8, is the remainder.
The digits in front of it, 73, are the quotient. Check: 10 times 73 is 730, add 8 makes 738.
items.question: Find the quotient and the remainder of 738 divided by 10.
items.checkpoint: Divided by ten, the ones digit is the remainder and the digits in front of it are the quotient.
items.misconception: Taking the first digit as the remainder because it is the one read first.

steps: A hundred takes the last two digits, so the cut goes just before the 5.
That gives quotient 82 and remainder 54. Check: 100 times 82 is 8200, add 54 makes 8254.
A thousand takes the last three digits, so the cut moves one place left: quotient 8, remainder 254.
items.question: Find the quotient and remainder of 8254 divided by 100, and then of 8254 divided by 1000.
items.checkpoint: Divided by a hundred, the last two digits are the remainder; divided by a thousand, the last three are.
items.misconception: Cutting off the same number of digits whatever the divisor, instead of one digit for each zero in it.

steps: A thousand takes the last three digits, so the cut goes between 41 and 007.
The last three digits read 0, 0 and 7, and the zeros in front change nothing, so the remainder is 7. Check: 1000 times 41 is 41,000, add 7 makes 41,007.
items.question: Find the quotient and remainder of 41,007 divided by 1000.
items.checkpoint: A remainder is a number, so zeros in front of it are not written.
items.misconception: Writing the remainder as 007 because those were the three digits cut off.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: 63 divided by 9 is 7. What is 630 divided by 9?
items.final_answer: 70, because 63 divided by 9 leaves nothing over, so ten times the dividend gives ten times the quotient

items.question: Find the quotient and remainder of 94 divided by 10.
In 5316 divided by 10, which digit is the remainder, and what is the quotient?
items.final_answer: The ones digit, 6, is the remainder, and the quotient is 531

items.question: 33 divided by 3 is 11. Find 330, 3300 and 33,000 divided by 3.
items.final_answer: 110, 1100 and 11,000, one more zero each time

items.question: Find the quotient and remainder of 6781 divided by 100.
Divide 38,265 by 1, by 10, by 100 and by 1000, giving each quotient and remainder.
Find the quotient and remainder of 70,009 divided by 1000, and write the remainder the way a number is written.
items.final_answer: 70 remainder 9. The last three digits read 009, and the zeros in front change nothing

items.question: Find the quotient and remainder of 4506 divided by 100, and then of 4506 divided by 1000.
items.final_answer: 45 remainder 6, and then 4 remainder 506. The last two digits read 06, which is the number 6

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: drops in from the right hand end, one digit for ten, two for a hundred, three for a thousand
takes the digits to the left of the bar and reads them as the quotient
takes the digits to the right of the bar and reads them as one number
lifts a zero standing in front of the remainder's other digits and shows it changes nothing
draws the number as bundles and loose sticks under the digit cards
adds a zero to the dividend a rung at a time with the divisor fixed
runs the same number divided by one, so four answers stand side by side

teaching_notes: Tie some sticks into bundles of ten and bundles of a hundred before the tool is opened, and ask how many whole tens a number makes and how many loose sticks are left. That is dividing by ten, and the written number already shows the answer: the loose sticks are the ones digit. The tool keeps the bundles and the digits on the stage together while the cut is made, so the rule is seen to be the bundles rather than a trick with the end of a number. Say the count of zeros aloud every time: one zero in ten, one digit cut off; two in a hundred, two digits; three in a thousand, three. The patterns at the start of this section work the same way from the other side, since a zero added to the dividend puts a zero on the quotient only while the divisor stays the same and the division leaves nothing over, so let a child add a zero to the divisor as well and see the quotient stay where it was. One row of the chapter's table for a thousand gives its remainder with a zero in front of sixteen. Copying the last three digits produces that, but a remainder is a number, and sixteen is written as sixteen. The box that divides one number four ways is worth doing on the tool with the trays left standing, so the four answers can be read in a row.
generation_prompt: Build a place splitting tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A number of up to five digits stands across the working area as digit cards, one to a column, each column under its own place heading. A splitter bar hangs above the cards with three settings reading ten, a hundred and a thousand, and each setting drops the bar that many digits in from the right hand end, one digit for each zero in the divisor. The digits left of the bar slide down into a quotient tray and the digits right of it into a remainder tray, and each tray reads its digits as one number. Where a zero stands in front of the remainder's other digits it is lifted off, set beside the tray at full size and shown to change nothing, and the remainder is written without it. A bundle view under the cards draws the same number as bundles of a thousand, a hundred and ten and loose sticks, with the whole bundles lighting with the quotient and the loose ones with the remainder. A pattern ladder at the left of the canvas starts from one division fact that leaves nothing over and adds a zero to the dividend a rung at a time, keeping the divisor fixed; if a zero is added to the divisor too, the quotient on that rung stays where it was and the rung says so. A one control runs the same number divided by one so four answers can stand side by side. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Count the zeros in the divisor. Cut off that many digits from the right. The digits in front are the quotient. The digits cut off are the remainder. Write the remainder as a number.
